thread.title: Nokia Should Weather Correction Better Than Most In Tech - Nokia Corporation (NYSE:NOK)

author: D.M. Martins Research
title: Nokia Should Weather Correction Better Than Most In Tech - Nokia Corporation (NYSE:NOK)

organizations.name: nokia should weather correction better than most in tech - nokia corporation

text:
Just about one year ago, I published an article proposing an alternative to the then-hot FANG portfolio . I called it NOAH, an acronym standing for Nokia ( NOK ), Oracle ( ORCL ), Apple ( AAPL ) and HP Inc. ( HPQ ), that also alluded to the famous tale of Noah's ark and the global flood. My main idea was to discuss a diversification approach to one's tech holdings in order to better face an eventual market pullback that, back then, I believed was just a matter of time.
Credit: How Stuff Works
Since then, and following the recent market jitters, the NOAH portfolio has under-performed the S&P 500 ( SPY ) by 310 bps on an annualized basis, as the chart below illustrates: 4.7% vs. the benchmark's 7.8%. Despite the recent, sharp pullback in AAPL, the only stock to have produced negative returns over the 15-month period was NOK: down 7% annualized, dividends included, vs. AAPL's +10%. If not for NOK, I calculate that the NOAH portfolio would have beaten the benchmark since September 2017 by an annualized 70 bps.
Source: DM Martins Research, using data from Yahoo Finance
I believe it is in the nature of most investors to shy away from stocks that have performed historically below expectations, perhaps the result of a common backward-looking bias. Those investors might be interested to know that, since the start of this year's third calendar quarter (i.e., roughly since the beginning of the current stock market correction), NOK has performed the best among all NOAH and FANG names along with the S&P 500 - and by a decent margin of at least five percentage points, in the case of the broad market.
But if I choose to take a forward-looking approach instead, I have even more reasons to believe that NOK should outperform its broad, tech peer group over the next few quarters - that is, in case we actually enter a textbook bear market or remain in correction territory for much longer.
This is not to say that NOK would not get "tossed around" a bit by negative investor sentiment, should bearishness in the markets take hold. In fact, NOK's 33% volatility (measured by one standard deviation of the annualized daily returns) since September 2017 suggests that this stock, subject to constant speculation regarding the length and extent of the upcoming 5G upgrade cycle, is far from a stable one. Instead, regardless of the path taken, I believe NOK should reach if not exceed my 24-month price target of $8/share, provided that it can deliver on the $0.50 in 2020 EPS that I believe the company can produce, even on a fairly conservative set of assumptions.
Below is my P&L model that I published right after Nokia's most recent earnings release. In it, I assume that revenues should slowly exit contraction mode and start producing low-single-digit growth that I believe is barely above market-wide trends. Supporting the top-line improvement is the reported "strong order backlog at the end of Q3" which, to be fair, does not seem to have translated into incremental earned revenues in a meaningful way as of yet. In my model, 2018 and 2019 revenues fall below current consensus , and I choose to stay conservative on my top-line projections on purpose.
Source: DM Martins Research, using data from company reports
Regarding profitability, I was encouraged to hear late last month about Nokia's plans to produce an extra €700 million in cost savings opportunities by 2020, about €200 million of which translating into higher gross profits. This latter piece alone, I estimate, should amount to 80 bps of gross margin improvement on top of previously-identified margin tailwinds (e.g. COGS efficiencies). On the op margin end, I project 14.8% in 2020 to land above the midpoint of the company's guidance range, as I believe Nokia has proven competent at cost management to keep opex under check.
In conclusion I don't believe that NOK is immune to the positive or negative effects of market-driven forces (e.g. global economic growth, inflation and interest rate expectations, investors' risk-on or risk-off attitudes). However, I think this stock is more likely than most in the tech world to trade, ultimately, on the fundamentals of the business as the network infrastructure refresh plays out through 2020 and beyond.
To that effect, I am fairly confident that Nokia should already have enough visibility into the long-cycle project pipeline to be able to project financial results 24 months out in the future with some level of precision. Judging by the recent narrative, it looks like Nokia's (usually conservative) management team has been excited about what is coming up next, which reinforces my convictions on my current earnings target.
Given the above, and considering that NOK has failed to leave the mid-$5/share range since early second quarter, I believe an investment in this stock at current levels is likely to produce better-than-average returns, particularly in the event of further stock market deterioration.
